stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: While cataloging over nine hundred beetle specimens collected from cloud forests in the Chiriquí Highlands of western ______ entomologist Annette Aiello discovered that thirty-seven of the species had never been formally described in any scientific publication.
explanation: The clause beginning with "While cataloging" is a dependent adverbial clause introduced by the subordinating conjunction "While." A comma is needed to separate this introductory dependent clause from the main clause beginning with "entomologist Annette Aiello discovered." Placing a period after "Panama" creates a sentence fragment because a dependent clause introduced by "While" cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. A semicolon is incorrect because semicolons join two independent clauses, and the "While" clause is dependent, not independent. Omitting punctuation entirely produces a run-on in which the dependent clause merges into the main clause without the required separation.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The cassowary, a large flightless bird native to the tropical forests of New Guinea and northeastern ______ plays a crucial ecological role by dispersing the seeds of more than two hundred and forty plant species through its digestive tract.
explanation: The phrase "a large flightless bird native to the tropical forests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia" is a nonrestrictive appositive renaming "The cassowary." Because the appositive is introduced by a comma after "cassowary," it must be closed with a matching comma before the main verb "plays." Omitting the closing comma fails to properly delimit the appositive, producing a structural error. Placing a period after "Australia" severs the subject from its predicate: "The cassowary, a large flightless bird...Australia." has no main verb, creating a fragment, while "Plays a crucial ecological role..." lacks a subject. A semicolon is incorrect because the subject with its appositive is not an independent clause—it has no predicate of its own.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The Chicxulub impactor — a bolide estimated at roughly eleven kilometers in diameter that struck the Yucatán Peninsula sixty-six million years ______ released energy equivalent to approximately ten billion nuclear detonations and ejected enough debris into the stratosphere to block sunlight for nearly two years.
explanation: The parenthetical "a bolide estimated at roughly eleven kilometers in diameter that struck the Yucatán Peninsula sixty-six million years ago" is introduced by an em-dash after "impactor." In standard English, a parenthetical opened with an em-dash must be closed with a matching em-dash before the sentence resumes. Using a comma to close a dash-opened parenthetical mixes incompatible punctuation marks, violating the convention that paired delimiters must match. A semicolon is incorrect because the material preceding it—a subject ("The Chicxulub impactor") interrupted by a parenthetical—does not constitute an independent clause with its own predicate. Placing a period after "ago" and beginning a new sentence with "It released" severs the subject from its predicate, leaving "The Chicxulub impactor — a bolide...ago." as a fragment with no main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The gallery's retrospective featured three landmark works of kinetic sculpture: Maren Jørgensen's 'Pendulum Chorus,' a suspended array of brass rods and tempered ______ Yuto Kobayashi's 'Salt Meridian,' a rotating assemblage of glass prisms, copper wire, and granulated sea salt; and Adaeze Okafor's 'Breathing Wall,' a pneumatic installation powered by barometric sensors and latex membranes.
explanation: The sentence presents a colon-introduced list of three items, each of which contains internal commas (for example, the appositive describing each sculpture). When list items contain their own commas, semicolons must be used to separate the items so that readers can distinguish item boundaries from internal punctuation. Using a comma to separate items in a list that already contains commas creates ambiguity about where one item ends and the next begins. Placing a period after "glass" breaks the colon-introduced list into a new sentence; "Yuto Kobayashi's 'Salt Meridian,' a rotating assemblage..." would lack a main verb and constitute a fragment. Introducing a second colon after the first one is non-standard in English—a colon introduces a single list or explanation, and nesting another colon within that structure violates standard punctuation conventions.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The collection of handwritten manuscripts belonging to the monastery's library ______ one of the most comprehensive archives of medieval pharmaceutical knowledge in Eastern Europe, containing detailed recipes for herbal remedies and surgical procedures that predate the oldest known European medical textbooks by at least two centuries.
explanation: The subject of the sentence is "The collection," a singular noun. The intervening prepositional phrases "of handwritten manuscripts" and "belonging to the monastery's library" do not change the number of the subject. A singular subject requires a singular verb, so "represents" is correct. The plural verb "represent" incorrectly treats "manuscripts" as the subject. "Are representing" fails on two counts: "are" does not agree with the singular subject, and the progressive aspect is inappropriate for a stative description of what the collection constitutes. "Have represented" uses the plural auxiliary "have" rather than the singular "has" required by the singular subject "collection."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: Although the ceramic tradition known as Jōmon pottery originated over sixteen thousand years ago in the Japanese archipelago, contemporary archaeologists now ______ that the intricate cord-marked patterns adorning these vessels served not merely as decoration but as a sophisticated system for regulating heat distribution during cooking.
explanation: The adverb "now" signals that the sentence describes what archaeologists currently think, requiring the present tense "believe." The past tense "believed" incorrectly shifts the timeframe to the past despite the explicit present-time marker "now"; a student who selects it may have been influenced by the historical context of the passage but overlooked the temporal signal. "Are believing" misapplies the progressive aspect to the stative verb "believe," which in standard English describes a mental state rather than an ongoing action and does not take the progressive form. "Had believed" is the past perfect tense, used to describe an action completed before another past event, which conflicts with the present-time framing established by "now."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The committee will award the Hargrove Fellowship to the candidate ______ the review panel determines has demonstrated the most innovative approach to addressing groundwater contamination in arid agricultural regions.
explanation: The relative pronoun must serve as the subject of "has demonstrated" in the clause "[who/whom] has demonstrated the most innovative approach." The intervening phrase "the review panel determines" is a parenthetical interpolation and does not change the grammatical role of the pronoun. Because the pronoun functions as the subject of "has demonstrated," the subjective case "who" is required. "Whom" is the objective case and would be appropriate only if the pronoun were the object of a verb or preposition; students who select it may mistakenly treat the pronoun as the object of "determines." "Which" is used for non-human antecedents and cannot refer to a person. "Whoever" is a generalized relative pronoun inappropriate in this context because the sentence specifies a definite antecedent ("the candidate"), and "the candidate whoever" produces a grammatically awkward construction.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The restoration plan requires that the wetland's natural hydrology be reestablished, that nonnative species currently dominating the understory ______ and that a monitoring protocol documenting changes in species diversity be implemented within the first two years of the project.
explanation: The verb "requires" triggers the mandative subjunctive in each of the three parallel "that" clauses. The first clause uses "be reestablished" and the third uses "be implemented," both in the subjunctive base form. Parallel structure and the subjunctive mandate demand that the second clause also use the base form "be removed." The indicative "are removed" breaks the subjunctive pattern required by "requires that" and disrupts the parallel structure, even though it might sound natural with the plural subject "species." "Will be removed" introduces the future tense, which is incompatible with the mandative subjunctive construction; the subjunctive already conveys the sense of a requirement or command without marking future time. "Have been removed" uses the present perfect, implying a completed action, which contradicts the forward-looking nature of a restoration plan that requires future actions.
